docs.title: iChidori-Crest
docs.text:
iChidori-Crest is a compact Raspberry Pi HAT designed for high-precision GNSS positioning and embedded applications. It integrates a Septentrio mosaic-G5 GNSS receiver module with an mPCIe interface for an LTE modem, onboard power management, SD card logging, and additional connectivity and expansion interfaces.

Designed for Raspberry Pi 4/5, iChidori-Crest provides a flexible hardware platform for RTK positioning, remote monitoring, and GNSS-based applications. It is available in variants — P1, P3, P3H, and P6 — sharing the same board hardware while offering different GNSS receiver capabilities.

docs.title: Powered by the Next-Generation Septentrio mosaic-G5
docs.text:
At the heart of iChidori-Crest is the Septentrio mosaic-G5, a new generation of ultra-compact, high-performance GNSS receiver modules. Combining multi-constellation, multi-frequency satellite tracking with centimeter-level RTK positioning, mosaic-G5 brings advanced positioning capabilities to space- and power-constrained systems.

Compared with the mosaic-X5, mosaic-G5 offers a 60% smaller module footprint and 40% lower power consumption, while maintaining high-precision positioning performance. Depending on the receiver variant, the series supports tracking of up to four frequencies, output rates of up to 100 Hz, and AIM+ Premium, advanced GNSS+ algorithms for enhanced resilience against interference and spoofing.

These capabilities make mosaic-G5 well suited for compact RTK systems, robotics, autonomous platforms, and other applications where positioning performance, reliability, size, and power efficiency are critical.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This guide covers the initial connection of the iChidori-Crest to a Window PC, installing required software, and performing basic configuration of the mosaic-G5 receiver using Septentrio RxControl.

The setup establishes a connection to the receiver, configures the antenna mode where supported, and enables GNSS data output on the receiver's serial ports.

By the end of this article we will have:

  • Connected the iChidori-Crest (mosaic-G5 receiver) to RxControl
  • Use the appropriate antenna mode for the board variant.
  • Enabled NMEA messages output on COM1
  • Enabled SBF output on COM2
  • Saved all settings as boot configuration

docs.title: Software Requirement
docs.text:
Install the following software on the Windows PC:

  • Septentrio USB Driver — required for Windows to recognize the mosaic-G5 receiver.
  • Septentrio RxTools — Software suit to control and monitor your GNSS receiver

Download RxTools and the ossociated documentation from the official Septentrio page: https://www.septentrio.com/en/products/gps-gnss-receiver-software/rxtools

Note

In the scope of these guide series, we primarily use RxControl and SBF Analyzer for the mosaic-G5 receiver's evaluation.

docs.title: Connect the iChidori-Crest to the PC
docs.text:
Connect the iChidori-Crest to the Windows PC using a USB Type-C cable.

After connecting the board, open Device Manager and check that the mosaic-G5 receiver's USB serial ports are detected.

Connection Troubleshooting

If the expected ports do not appear, check the USB connection and confirm that the Septentrio USB driver is installed correctly. If necessary, reconnect the board or try a different USB Type-C cable that supports data transfer.

docs.title: Connect RxControl to the Receiver
docs.text:
Once the USB ports are detected, create a connection in RxControl. On first launch with a new mosaic-G5 receiver, follow these steps to create a new connection:

  1. Open RxControl application
  2. Select File → Change Connection
  3. Select Serial Connection → Create New → Next
  4. Under Select Port, choose the receiver's USB port. In this setup, select USB Port 1
  5. Enter a Connection Name — for example: mosaic_g5_p6_3754
  6. Click Finish to create the connection

The receiver should now be accessible through RxControl.

docs.title: Confirm and Configure The Antenna Mode
docs.text:
The mosaic-G5 supports single-antenna and dual-antenna operation. The available modes depend on the iChidori-Crest variant.

Variant support

  • P1, P3: Single Antenna only
  • P3H, P6: Single Antenna and Dual Antenna

Use the Expert Console in RxControl to check the current mode and configure the receiver if needed. Open the Expert Console from the RxControl toolbar and enter the following commands individually. Choose the mode appropriate for the board variant and antenna setup.

  • getFrontendMode — query the current antenna mode
  • setFrontendMode, SingleAnt — configure single-antenna mode at the next reboot
  • setFrontendMode, DualAnt — configure dual-antenna (heading) mode at the next reboot
  • exeCopyConfigFile, Current, Boot — save the configuration to the boot file
  • exeResetReceiver, Hard, none — reboot to apply

Note

The antenna mode takes effect after the receiver is restarted. If a mode change is required, save the configuration and restart the receiver after completing the remaining settings.

docs.title: Enable - COM1, COM2 Output
docs.text:
Output NMEA GGA on COM1 - mosaic G5 on COM1 at 1Hz.

Open Communication → Output Settings → NMEA Output. Configure on Stream 1:

Field Value Port COM1 Message GGA Interval 1 sec (1 Hz)

Enable SBF Output on COM2 - mosaic G5 on COM2 at 1 Hz.

Navigate to: Communication → Output Settings → SBF Output. Configure on Stream 1:

Field Value Port COM2 Blocks PVTGeodetic, MeasEpoch,... Interval 1 sec (1 Hz)

docs.title: Save The Boot Configuration
docs.text:
After completing all settings, save the full configuration so it is restored after every power cycle.

To save the current configuration as boot configuration, open File->Copy Configuration, and select Current as source, Boot as target. Click Apply and OK to save.

Warning

Always save to Boot configuration after any change. Settings not saved to Boot will be lost after power cycle.

docs.title: Optional — Configure the GPIO LEDs
docs.text:
The iChidori-Crest provides two onboard LEDs controlled by GPIO1 and GPIO2 of the mosaic-G5. These indicators can help monitor receiver status during evaluation and field testing.

GPIO Function Description GPIO1 nRTKLED LED ON when RTK Fixed GPIO2 nPVTLED LED ON when PVT solution available

Open Navigation → Receiver Operation -> GPIO, set each GPIO to the corresponding function, then save to Boot configuration.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this article, we completed the first connection of the iChidori-Crest to a PC using Septentrio RxControl. Starting from a fresh setup, we established a USB connection to the mosaic-G5 receiver, confirmed and setting the antenna operating mode, configured the receiver to output data on COM1 and COM2. All settings were saved to Boot configuration to ensure they persist across power cycles.

These output streams will be used for the next evaluation, where we explore RTK positioning and data logging on this GNSS receiver.

In the next guide, we will configure the iChidori-Crest as an RTK Rover using RxControl.

Next: Configuring mosaic G5 as an RTK Rover →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The iChidori-Crest supports LTE connectivity through a cellular modem installed in its mPCIe slot. When combined with a Raspberry Pi, it provides Internet connectivity for the system.

The LTE configuration process depends on the modem being used, as setup procedures and carrier settings may vary between modem models.

This guide demonstrates a complete LTE setup using the Quectel EC21-J modem, from initial hardware detection and SIM configuration to automatic connection at startup.

The configuration follows the standard Linux networking stack:

  • ModemManager detects and manages the cellular modem, including SIM status and mobile network registration.
  • NetworkManager configures and manages the LTE connection profile and network interface.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi 4 with the iChidori-Crest installed.
  • Raspberry Pi OS.
  • Quectel EC21-J installed in the mPCIe slot.
  • Active nano-SIM card inserted into the iChidori-Crest SIM slot.
  • LTE antenna connected to the modem's antenna port.
  • Suitable 5 V power supply for the Raspberry Pi.
  • A USB Type-C cable connecting the Raspberry Pi to the iChidori-Crest's USB port.

A valid SIM subscription, compatible carrier settings, and sufficient cellular coverage are required for Internet access.

Example Configuration

This guide uses the Quectel EC21-J with a mineo SIM operating on the au (KDDI) network. The APN and authentication settings may differ depending on the SIM provider and must be configured accordingly.

docs.title: Hardware Setup
docs.text:
Note

The LAN cable is used only to access the Raspberry Pi via SSH during the initial setup and configuration. It is not required for LTE connectivity.

docs.title: 1. Verify LTE Modem Detection
docs.text: After powering on the Raspberry Pi with the LTE modem installed on the iChidori-Crest, verify that the modem is detected over USB.

docs.title: Check USB Detection
docs.text:
Execute the following commands:

lsusb
ls /dev/ttyUSB* 2>/dev/null

Example output:

The device ID and bus information may differ depending on the hardware and USB configuration.

Quectel EC21-J USB Serial Interfaces

The EC21-J exposes four USB serial interfaces. Each serves a specific purpose:

Interface Function Description /dev/ttyUSB0 Modem / diagnostics General modem control and diagnostic functions. /dev/ttyUSB1 GNSS NMEA output GNSS data output, if supported and enabled in the modem configuration. /dev/ttyUSB2 AT commands Primary interface for sending AT commands. /dev/ttyUSB3 AT commands Secondary AT command interface.

The interface mapping above is based on the tested EC21-J configuration. Actual assignments may vary depending on modem firmware and USB configuration. Verify the available interfaces on the target device before use.

GNSS and LTE USB Interfaces

The Septentrio mosaic-G5 GNSS module typically appears as /dev/ttyACM0 and /dev/ttyACM1, while the Quectel LTE modem uses /dev/ttyUSBx interfaces.

These device names identify different hardware interfaces and should not be confused.

docs.title: 2. Verify Modem Communication and SIM Status
docs.text: This step verifies communication with the Quectel EC21-J modem, checks the SIM card and mobile network status, and prepares the modem for LTE connection configuration.

docs.title: Install an AT Command Terminal
docs.text:
AT commands can be sent to the LTE modem through its AT command interface using a serial terminal or other serial communication tools.

This guide uses minicom as an example. Install it if it is not already available:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install minicom -y

AT Command Terminal Options

This guide uses minicom, but any serial terminal tool works. Common alternatives include screen and tio. The choice depends on personal preference.

Next, open the EC21-J AT command interface:

sudo minicom -D /dev/ttyUSB2 -b 115200

The example uses /dev/ttyUSB2 as the AT command interface. Confirm the port assignment according to the USB serial interface mapping described in Step 1.

If the characters you type are not displayed, enable local echo by pressing Ctrl+A, followed by E.

docs.title: Verify Modem and SIM Status
docs.text:
Enter the following AT commands to confirm that the modem and SIM are ready:

AT Command Purpose Expected Response AT Verify communication OK AT+CPIN? Check SIM card status +CPIN: READY AT+CIMI Read SIM IMSI Numeric IMSI value AT+CSQ Check signal strength +CSQ: <rssi>,<ber>

docs.title: Verify Network Registration
docs.text:
Execute the following commands:

AT+CEREG?
AT+COPS?
AT Command Purpose AT+CEREG? Check LTE/EPS network registration status. AT+COPS? Check the selected mobile network operator.

A response containing +CEREG: 0,1 confirms that the modem is registered on its home network.

Example output:

Network Registration

If the modem is not registered, verify SIM activation, antenna connection, signal strength, and carrier coverage before proceeding.

After verifying modem and SIM status, exit Minicom. The APN settings will be configured in the next step through NetworkManager.

docs.title: 3. Install and Configure ModemManager
docs.text: ModemManager handles modem detection and coordinates with NetworkManager to manage the LTE connection.

docs.title: Install ModemManager
docs.text:
Install ModemManager if it is not already available:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install modemmanager -y

Verify that both tools are available:

nmcli --version
mmcli --version

Raspberry Pi OS includes NetworkManager by default, so no additional installation is required.

Example output:

docs.title: Verify ModemManager Detects the Modem
docs.text:
Run the following command to check whether ModemManager detects the LTE modem:

mmcli -L

Expected output:

/org/freedesktop/ModemManager1/Modem/0 [QUALCOMM INCORPORATED] QUECTEL Mobile Broadband Module

Troubleshooting: No modems were found

During testing, mmcli -L returned No modems were found, even though the EC21-J was installed and powered.

1. Verify USB device detection

First, check whether the Raspberry Pi recognizes the modem over USB:

lsusb | grep -i quectel

Example output:

Bus 001 Device 005: ID 2c7c:0121 Quectel Wireless Solutions Co., Ltd. EC21 LTE modem

This confirms that the Linux kernel recognizes the EC21-J as a USB device. However, USB detection alone does not guarantee that ModemManager can manage the modem.

2. Inspect udev properties

Check the udev properties of the modem's serial interface:

udevadm info /dev/ttyUSB2 | grep -i "ID_VENDOR\|ID_MODEL\|ID_MM"

During testing, the following properties were observed:

E: ID_MODEL=Android
E: ID_MODEL_ID=0121
E: ID_VENDOR=Android
E: ID_VENDOR_ID=2c7c
E: ID_VENDOR_FROM_DATABASE=Quectel Wireless Solutions Co., Ltd.
E: ID_MODEL_FROM_DATABASE=EC21 LTE modem

The EC21-J KDDI firmware reports Android as its USB vendor and product descriptor strings, while its USB vendor and product IDs identify the device as Quectel EC21 (2c7c:0121).

In this configuration, the device was not tagged as a ModemManager candidate (ID_MM_CANDIDATE=1). This prevented ModemManager from detecting the modem.

3. Apply a custom udev rule

Create a udev rule to identify the EC21-J using its USB vendor and product IDs instead of the descriptor strings:

echo 'ATTRS{idVendor}=="2c7c", ATTRS{idProduct}=="0121", ENV{ID_MM_CANDIDATE}="1"' \
  | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-quectel-ec21.rules

Reload the udev rules and restart ModemManager:

sudo udevadm control --reload-rules
sudo udevadm trigger
sudo systemctl restart ModemManager
sleep 5

4. Verify modem detection

Run the detection command again:

mmcli -L

Expected output:

/org/freedesktop/ModemManager1/Modem/0 [QUALCOMM INCORPORATED] QUECTEL Mobile Broadband Module

The EC21-J should now be detected by ModemManager.

Note: This workaround was verified with the EC21-J KDDI firmware variant. Other EC21 firmware versions or modem models may not require this additional udev rule.

After successful detection, retrieve the modem details to check its status and available interfaces:

mmcli -m 0

Example output:

docs.title: 4. Create the LTE Connection Profile
docs.text:
Create a connection profile with the APN credentials. This example uses mineo on the au (KDDI) network:

sudo nmcli connection add \
  type gsm \
  ifname "*" \
  con-name "lte-mineo" \
  apn "mineo.jp" \
  user "mineo@k-opti.com" \
  password "mineo"

Expected output:

Connection 'lte-mineo' (...) successfully added.

APN Settings

The apn, user, and password values must match the SIM provider's configuration. Contact the carrier or refer to its documentation for the correct APN and authentication settings.

docs.title: Activate the Connection
docs.text:
Activate the LTE connection profile:

sudo nmcli connection up lte-mineo

Expected output:

Connection successfully activated (D-Bus active path: /org/freedesktop/NetworkManager/ActiveConnection/5)

docs.title: Verify the Network Interface
docs.text:
Check the LTE network interface:

ip addr show wwan0

The wwan0 interface should have an assigned IP address.

Example output:

3: wwan0: <POINTOPOINT,MULTICAST,NOARP,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ...
    inet 100.124.165.x/30 brd 100.124.165.x scope global noprefixroute wwan0

The assigned IP address may differ depending on the carrier and network configuration.

docs.title: Test Internet Connectivity
docs.text:
First, test IP connectivity:

ping -c 3 8.8.8.8

Example output:

64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=119 time=4.29 ms
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=2 ttl=119 time=2.96 ms
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=3 ttl=119 time=3.37 ms

Next, verify DNS resolution:

getent hosts google.com

A successful response indicates that the hostname can be resolved.

LTE Connection Established

If the LTE interface is up, an IP address is assigned, and the connectivity tests succeed, the Raspberry Pi is connected to the Internet over LTE.

docs.title: 6. Configure Automatic Connection at Startup
docs.text:
NetworkManager supports automatic connection activation through its connection profile settings.

Enable autoconnect for the LTE connection:

sudo nmcli connection modify lte-mineo connection.autoconnect yes

Verify the setting:

nmcli connection show lte-mineo | grep autoconnect

Expected output:

connection.autoconnect:                 yes

NetworkManager automatically attempts to activate the connection profile at startup and reconnects when possible if the connection is interrupted. No additional systemd service configuration is required.

Example output:

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This guide demonstrated how to configure LTE connectivity on the iChidori-Crest using the Quectel EC21-J modem and a mineo SIM on the au (KDDI) network.

Once configured, the Raspberry Pi can access the Internet through the LTE network without requiring a wired LAN connection.

The same configuration approach can be adapted for other supported LTE modems and SIM providers by adjusting the modem-specific settings and APN credentials.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
So far in this guide series, we have been working with the iChidori-Crest connected to a PC for quick evaluation. This guide explains how to use iChidori-Crest with a Rasberry Pi.

The iChidori-Crest connects to the Raspberry Pi through its 40-pin GPIO header. For pin mapping details, see 40-Pin Header Assignments.

In this guide, we will use the USB interface of the mosaic-G5 receiver. The Raspberry Pi communicates with the mosaic-G5 via USB, while MRTKLIB's mrtk relay is used to stream NTRIP corrections to the receiver and attempt to achieve an RTK Fixed solution.

About MRTKLIB: Modernized RTKLIB for Next-Generation GNSS

This guide uses mrtk relay from MRTKLIB — a modern GNSS positioning library built on RTKLIB, adding PPP, PPP-AR, and PPP-RTK (CLAS/MADOCA) support. If you have not yet installed MRTKLIB, refer to the MRTKLIB Documentation before proceeding.

docs.title: Step 1 — Configure mosaic-G5 USB Output
docs.text:
Note

This step configures additional data outputs for monitoring and post-test analysis. It is recommended for evaluation purposes.

Open RxControl and establish a connection with the mosaic-G5 (see Basic Setup if needed).

Navigate to Communication → Output Settings → NMEA Output and configure Stream 1 as follows:

Field Value Port USB1 Message GGA (or as required) Interval 1 sec (or as required)

Next, navigate to Communication → Output Settings → SBF Output and configure Stream 1 as follows:

Field Value Port USB2 Blocks PVTGeodetic, MeasEpoch (or as required) Interval 1 sec (or as required)

Click Apply and OK after each setting.

Don't forward to Save to boot configuration for the next power cycle.

docs.title: Step 2 — Verify mosaic-G5 USB Ports on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
With the iChidori-Crest attached on Raspberry Pi and powered, the mosaic-G5 will enumerate two USB serial devices on the Raspberry Pi. These correspond to the USB1 and USB2 ports configured in the previous step.

SSH into the Raspberry Pi and run the following command to confirm both ports are detected:

ls /dev/ttyACM*

If the devices do not appear, check that the USB-C cable between the iChidori-Crest and the Raspberry Pi is connected.

Verify the USB data stream

Before proceeding to the next step, confirm that data is actively streaming from both USB ports. Use mrtk relay to read directly from each serial port and print the output to the terminal:

~/Projects/MRTKLIB/build/mrtk relay --input serial://ttyACM0:115200 --output -

~/Projects/MRTKLIB/build/mrtk relay --input serial://ttyACM1:115200 --output -

You should see SBF/NMEA sentences scrolling continuously in the terminal like this terminal image:

docs.title: Step 3 — Forward NTRIP Corrections to mosaic-G5
docs.text:
With the data streams verified on USB ports, we can now stream RTCM3 correction data from an NTRIP caster to the mosaic-G5 receiver via ttyACM0:

~/Projects/MRTKLIB/build/mrtk relay \
  --input ntrip://guest:guest@ntrip.aitoya.net:2101/MOSAIC-RTCM3 \
  --output serial://ttyACM0:115200

Use your own NTRIP caster

The example above uses the Aitoya NTRIP caster for reference. Replace the host, port, mountpoint, username and password with your own caster credentials before running.

Once running, mrtk relay will continuously receive RTCM3 packets from the caster and forward them to the mosaic-G5 in real time. Leave this process running in the terminal and open a new terminal window to proceed to the next step.

docs.title: Step 4 — Verify RTK Fix
docs.text:
With NTRIP corrections streaming to the mosaic-G5, the receiver will begin processing them and improve its position solution — RTK Fixed. Open a new terminal and monitor the NMEA GGA output to track the fix status:

stty -F /dev/ttyACM0 115200 && cat /dev/ttyACM0

Watch the fix quality field in the $GNGGA sentence (the 6th comma-separated value):

Fix Quality Status 0 No fix 1 Standalone GNSS fix 2 DGPS fix 5 RTK Float — corrections received, ambiguity not yet resolved 4 RTK Fixed ✓ — centimeter-level accuracy achieved

RTK Fixed GGA output:

Note

At this point, the mosaic-G5 is outputting NMEA and SBF data via USB in RTK Fixed state. If you wish to log this data for further evaluation, you can use mrtk relay to capture each stream to a file:

# Log NMEA from ttyACM0
~/Projects/MRTKLIB/build/mrtk relay --input serial://ttyACM0:115200 --output file://<path/to/output>.nma

# Log SBF from ttyACM1
~/Projects/MRTKLIB/build/mrtk relay --input serial://ttyACM1:115200 --output file://<path/to/output>.sbf

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This article demonstrated how to use the iChidori-Crest + Raspberry Pi as an RTK rover, receiving NTRIP corrections over the network and achieving a centimeter-level RTK Fixed solution.

The procedure covered:

  1. Configuring the mosaic-G5 USB output for NMEA and SBF data streams for data logging purpose.
  2. Verifying USB serial port detection on the Raspberry Pi.
  3. Forwarding RTCM3 corrections from an NTRIP caster to the mosaic-G5 using mrtk relay.
  4. Monitoring NMEA GGA output to confirm RTK Fixed status.

With RTK Fixed achieved, the iChidori-Crest is ready for field deployment in applications requiring centimeter-level positioning accuracy.

Next: LTE Connectivity with the iChidori-Crest →

docs.title: Configuring mosaic-G5 as an RTK Rover
Overview
docs.text:
This guide explains how to configure the mosaic-G5 as an RTK rover using the built-in NTRIP Forwarder in Septentrio RxControl.

The NTRIP Forwarder connects to an NTRIP caster and forwards RTCM3 correction data to the receiver. With a suitable GNSS antenna setup and valid correction data, the rover can achieve an RTK Fixed solution.

By the end of this guide, the receiver will be connected to an NTRIP correction source, and its positioning status will be checked in RxControl.

docs.title: Setup Requirements
docs.text:
Before starting, prepare the following:

  • iChidori-Crest connected to PC using USB Type-C cable.
  • RxControl installed, with a connection to the mosaic-G5 established. See Basic Setup for the initial configuration.
  • An active NTRIP caster account, including the server address, port, and mountpoint where required.
  • Ensure that a GNSS antenna (or two, for Dual Antenna mode) connected to iChidori-Crest and placed antenna in open-sky view

Correction Service

The caster address, port, mountpoint, and authentication requirements depend on the correction service being used. The settings below are an example and should be replaced if a different NTRIP service is used.

docs.title: Configure the NTRIP Forwarder
docs.text:
With the iChidori-Crest connected in RxControl, navigate to the RXControl NTRIP Forwarder:

Open Communication → RXControl NTRIP Forwarder. Click Edit:

Enter NTRIP caster details:

Field Value Caster ntrip.aitoya.net Port 2101 Mountpoint MOSAIC-RTCM3

Click Connect to begin streaming correction data to the receiver.

docs.title: Verify the RTK Solution
docs.text:
After connecting the NTRIP Forwarder, monitor the positioning status in RxControl.

The receiver may initially report a standalone solution while acquiring satellites or before correction data is applied. As valid corrections become available, the solution may progress to RTK Float and then RTK Fixed.

Status Description No Fix No GNSS solution Standalone GNSS fix, no corrections DGPS Differential correction applied RTK Float Corrections received, ambiguity not resolved RTK Fixed Full RTK solution — centimeter-level accuracy ✓

Wait for the receiver to reach RTK Fixed and check that the solution remains stable before proceeding with further evaluation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The mosaic-G5 has been configured as an RTK rover using the NTRIP Forwarder in RxControl. After connecting to the correction service, the receiver's positioning status can be monitored to confirm whether an RTK Fixed solution has been achieved.

This method provides a straightforward way to evaluate rover operation directly from a PC before integrating the correction stream into a project.

Tip

The RxControl NTRIP Forwarder is convenient for initial testing. For more advanced correction-data routing or network configurations, consider the Data Link Tools included in RxTools.

The next guide covers receiver data logging and the analysis of recorded GNSS data.

Next: Data Logging →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The mosaic-G5 supports several ways to record GNSS receiver data for evaluation and debugging. This guide introduces two logging methods available when using the iChidori-Crest:

  • PC logging: Record receiver data directly to a PC using RxControl.
  • SD card logging: Store receiver data on the onboard SD card for standalone operation without a continuously connected PC.

Both methods can be used to record SBF binary data and NMEA messages. The appropriate method depends on the test setup and how the recorded data will be retrieved and analyzed.

docs.title: Method 1 — Log SBF/NMEA Messages to PC via RxControl
docs.text:
RxControl includes a built-in logger that can record the SBF binary stream and/or NMEA ASCII stream directly to a file on your PC.

Open Logging → RxControl Logging to open the Logger window.

Configure the log file name and select which SBF/NMEA messages to record, then click Start Logging.

Logging status

Closing the Logger window does not stop logging. Logging status is shown in the RxControl status bar:

  • Icon active → logging in progress
  • Icon inactive → logging stopped

To stop logging, return to Logging → RxControl Logging and click Stop.

docs.title: Method 2 — Log SBF/NMEA Messages to Internal SD Card (DSK1)
docs.text:
The iChidori-Crest features a built-in SD card slot, recognized by the mosaic-G5 as DSK1. This enables autonomous data logging in the evaluation without a connected PC.

SD Card Format

Before inserting the SD card into the iChidori-Crest, format it as FAT32. The receiver must recognize the card as DSK1 before SD card logging can be configured.

To configure SBF logging to the SD card, navigate to: Communication → Output Settings → SBF Output

Select DSK1 in the Ports row, choose the SBF messages to log, and set the output interval.

Click Apply and OK to save.

Tip: Download data from SD card

RxControl supports downloading logged data directly from the SD card to your PC — no need to physically remove it from the iChidori-Crest. Open Logging → Download Internal Files to retrieve SBF/NMEA log files from DSK1.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this article, we explored two data logging approaches for the mosaic-G5 on the iChidori-Crest board. Logging to PC via RxControl is convenient for quick evaluation sessions, while logging to the onboard SD card enables standalone field evaluation without a connected PC.

Note

SD card logging is intended for evaluation and debugging purposes. It is not recommended for production or deployed systems.

Next: Connect to a Raspberry Pi →

docs.title: Appendix A
docs.text: This appendix provides a technical comparison of the mosaic-G5 variants and selected GNSS receivers.

docs.title: 40-Pin Header (J1)
docs.text:
iChidori-Crest connects to the Raspberry Pi via the standard 40-pin GPIO header.

Connector type: 2×20, 2.54 mm Pin socket

Mating connector: Raspberry Pi 4/5 Model B built-in 40-pin GPIO header

docs.title: UART Interfaces Summary
docs.text:
Interface Raspberry Pi Mosaic G5 LTE Module G5 UART UART0/1 (GPIO14/15) COM1 — G5 UART UART4 (GPIO8/9/10/11) COM2 — LTE UART UART3 (GPIO4/5/6/7) — UART

Serial port configuration

Raspberry Pi 4/5 has UART0–UART5, but most are disabled by default and require additional configuration.

To enable UART on GPIO14/GPIO15 (TXD/RXD) for mosaic-G5 COM1:

  1. Run sudo raspi-config
  2. Select Interface Options → Serial Port
  3. Set Login shell over serial → No
  4. Set Serial port hardware → Yes
  5. Exit and reboot

After reboot, verify which UART type is assigned to the primary serial port:

ls -l /dev/serial0

On Raspberry Pi 4/5, /dev/ttyAMA* represents PL011 UARTs and /dev/ttyS* represents the mini UART.

Use a PL011 UART (/dev/ttyAMA*) for communication with the mosaic-G5. PL011 UARTs have a dedicated clock and provide stable baud rates at higher speeds. The mini UART (/dev/ttyS0) shares the CPU clock and is not recommended for GNSS applications.

If serial0 points to /dev/ttyS0, reassign it to PL011 by adding the following line to /boot/firmware/config.txt:

dtoverlay=disable-bt

This disables Bluetooth and frees the PL011 UART for GPIO14/GPIO15. Reboot and verify again:

ls -l /dev/serial0

Confirm that serial0 now points to /dev/ttyAMA0 before proceeding.

Connector type: USB Type-C, USB 2.0

The USB-C connector serves as the primary power supply and data interface.

docs.title: GNSS Antenna Connectors
docs.text:
iChidori-Crest provides two MMCX antenna connectors for the mosaic-G5 receiver.

Antenna supply voltage

Both ports supply V_ANT = 3.3 V DC to power active GNSS antennas.

docs.title: Antenna Mode Setting
docs.text:
iChidori-Crest is offered in variants that differ in antenna capability:

Variant Antenna Mode P1, P3 Single-antenna only P3H, P6 Single-antenna or dual-antenna (heading)

Use the following commands to check or configure the antenna mode:

  • getFrontendMode — query the current antenna mode
  • setFrontendMode, SingleAnt — configure single-antenna mode at the next reboot
  • setFrontendMode, DualAnt — configure dual-antenna (heading) mode at the next reboot
  • exeCopyConfigFile, Current, Boot — save the configuration to the boot file
  • exeResetReceiver, Hard, none — reboot to apply

Connect an active antenna to ANT_1 (MAIN). The ANT_1 input is DC-biased and ESD-protected; an active antenna can be connected directly without additional components. Leave ANT_2 (AUX) open when operating in single-antenna mode.

docs.title: SD Logging (J4)
docs.text:
A physical SD card slot is provided for direct on-board logging by the mosaic-G5 receiver.

Note

This SD logging capability is intended for evaluation and debugging purposes only; it is not recommended for use in production/deployed systems.

docs.title: SIM Card (J10)
docs.text:
The board provides a Nano SIM socket for the LTE module.

SIM slot on the LTE card

If the installed LTE card has its own SIM slot, the SIM can be inserted directly into that slot instead of the Nano SIM socket on the iChidori-Crest. This allows SIM sizes other than Nano (for example Micro or Mini, depending on the card) to be used. The supported SIM types therefore depend on the LTE card in use.

docs.title: LTE Modems Tested
docs.text:
The iChidori-Crest has been tested with the following LTE modems:

LTE Modem Category Interface Quectel EC21-J LTE Cat 1 USB + UART Quectel BG96 LTE Cat M1 / NB-IoT USB + UART

Other LTE modem should be work, provided they use a compatible mPCIe form factor and interface configuration.

Note

The mPCIe LTE I²C interface is not connected in the current board revision. Use USB or UART for LTE communication.
